title: What the Carbon Kept
blurb: Mags finally opens the union's thirty-year-old box, and what the carbon copy says about the Corn Exchange keeper has Ila walking into her father's lock-up.

blocks.text: "No," I say.
It's out before I've finished deciding, the way my truest sentences always are. Gervase Vosper keeps his gloved hand on the door he's holding open for me, and he doesn't move it an inch.
"No to the notebooks," he asks pleasantly, "or no to the post?"
"Both. You can't give me the post, and the notebooks aren't mine to bring."
"Nothing worth having is ever yours to bring, Ila. That's what makes it a favour."
His eyes go, just once, to my coat pocket, where my phone sits full to the last picture with his drawer. Then they come back to my face, kind as a family doctor's.

"The offer keeps till the end of the month," he says. "So do I. And Ila? Do give Orla my regards." He tilts his head. "Or perhaps don't. She'd only ask how we met. And then you'd have to tell her everything else, wouldn't you?"
He says good night. The door closes so softly I barely hear the latch.
I go down the Allocation stair on my own. Bev has gone home and the stair is just a stair. I hold the rail the whole way, because my knees have decided they're somebody else's.

He knows I haven't told Orla. He knows why I can't. If I tell her Vosper wants her notebooks, I have to tell her who sells Ferdie his luck, and whose hands I watched tie her snare on the ironmonger's step. One name opens all of it.
So I don't go to Nettlecombe. I go to the union hall, where Mags's branch meeting is finishing, and I wait on the bench by the coats until the last Porter has gone.
"The Corn Exchange," I say. "Thirty years ago. Something that size had a keeper, and keepers that size are always yours. Does the union keep a copy?"
Mags looks at me for a long time.

"We keep a copy of every docket a member's put his hand to," she says, "since the seventies. That one's in the strongroom. Nobody's opened it." She buttons her donkey jacket. "Ask me again when I've slept."
She doesn't sleep on it for one night. She sleeps on it for eleven.

The union strongroom smells of carbon paper and damp. Mags stands with both hands on a docket box nobody has opened in thirty years. Someone has written on its end, in brown ink gone soft with age: Corn Exchange.
"If I open this," she says, "the membership owns whatever's in it. All of it."
There are eight days left on Vosper's clock. I've been talking for eleven. For once I don't say a word.
Mags lays her palm flat on the lid, the way she ends an argument, and lifts it.

There's only one thing inside: a docket copy on thin blue carbon, with a strand-rate sheet pinned behind it. Mags unpins the sheet, reads the card first, and turns it so I can see the top half. She keeps her thumb across the bottom.

The carbon is faint, but it's all there. The site: the Corn Exchange. The knot: worn, holding the building up. The count, certified by Standards: twelve. Ordered by H. Tregear, Deputy Sexton. Untier: Master Lettice Orpwood, under an extraordinary warrant. And a line in the remarks box, pressed hard enough to come through clearly: Site not clear. Two knotters inside the knot.
"They untied it," I say, "with two knotters inside."
"Says so." Mags's voice is very flat.

She hands me the strand-rate sheet. It's what the union bills from: Standards swings the keeper after the fall, the union is paid by the strand, so the union gets a carbon of the swing. Fell on keeper: five strands. Rate paid on five. And in the margin, small, in a neat hand that has gone through the carbon the way a careful pen always does, because carbon paper doesn't know what's meant to stay on the top sheet:
Slack short by 7. No further action. H.T.
H. Tregear. Small and grey, hair pinned flat, thanking me for my patience outside the Standards door. Deputy Sexton then. Sexton now.

"My first year as steward," Mags says, without looking up, "the old steward showed me this shelf. He said, that one we don't open. I asked why. He said, because the membership signed it, and if it's bad, it's ours." She taps the margin. "Twelve undone and five fell. Seven strands walked off on their own, and Management wrote 'no further action' on it like it was a late tram."

I know where seven went. Seven went into a broken chest during a twelve-minute dwell, and they've kept a man's heart catching for thirty years. That's Orla's crime and Orla's to tell, so I hold my tongue, and it's the hardest thing I've done all month.
"Who was the keeper?" I ask instead.

Mags lifts her thumb and reads the bottom of the card herself. She doesn't say anything. She reads it for much longer than a name takes. Then she looks up at me, at my face, carefully, the way I've seen her match a signature against the union roll.
She folds the bottom third of the card under and runs her thumbnail down the crease.

"Members' particulars are confidential," she says. "'No officer of the Society shall show a member's particulars to any person not of the Society.' You're Management, love. Suspended Management, but Management."
"Mags, I need to know who..."
Her palm comes down flat on the folded card. That's the end of it.

I want to give her something back, because she's just opened a box she's been afraid of for thirty years, and all I've done is stand in her strongroom asking for more. So I give her the only thing I have.
"The last docket in Vosper's book," I say. "Your name. I think I can keep you safe from it. Give me a day."
"Don't promise the membership what you can't deliver."
"I'm not promising the membership," I say. "I'm promising you."
She looks at me like I'm something she hasn't decided whether to frame or throw away.
"One day," she says.
Nettlecombe, after lunch, under a sky that can't make up its mind. Orla is kneeling at the end of a bed of field stones with her sleeves pushed up.
"Abbot," she says, and taps a grey stone the size of a loaf. "Three. Been in that bed longer than you've been alive. Fid."
I've drilled on these stones every day for ten weeks, the twos and the ones, and the cord in the shed until my fingertips went hard. I've never been handed a three.

I sign the docket first, in my own hand, as keeper. I have no licence. Under the Act this is unlicensed knotting, a crime, the same crime as the cobble, only heavier. I know it word for word, and I sign anyway, and my hand only shakes on the B.
Then I work.

It's slow. A strand comes free under the fid like a thread out of wet wool, and then the next, and the next is the stubborn one, and I don't stop, because an interruption would snarl it, and a snarl would misfire around Abbot until someone finished it. If three were above my reach, one strand would fall on me at once, whatever the docket says. I wait for it the whole last minute.
Nothing falls. Abbot goes quiet under my hand.
"Three," says Orla.

She takes a notebook out of her jacket pocket. It's small and black, with an elastic band round it and a pencil pushed down the spine, and she writes something in it with the stub. My whole body goes still, as if the notebook might hear me.
"Something wrong with my book, Clerk?"
"It's a nice book," I say.
"It's a book." She snaps the band back on and pockets it. "Three minutes of dwell. Watch."

She turns to the fence, where the starlings sit in their tidy rows, and her hands move fast and certain over the stone. She catches all three strands before the dwell runs out, with three of the birds as the loose strands in sight, and ties them straight back onto Abbot. Then she signs a new docket as keeper of that, folds it into her pocket beside the notebook, and pats the stone. "Back to bed."
"So nothing falls on me," I say.
"Nothing falls on you today. I'm keeper. Slack's never less, Clerk. Only somewhere else."
I sit back on my heels in the wet grass. Reach three. Tie one. I've wanted this number for four years and ten weeks, and now that I have it, all I can think about is what one tie can do.
"I can tie one," I say. "That means I can save Mags."
"Can you."

"There's a book of dockets. A seller's book." I don't say whose, and Orla doesn't ask, the way she didn't ask about Ferdie. "The last docket in it is for Mags Danquah, the steward, and it isn't signed. Nobody's signed as keeper. So the snare isn't tied yet. If I untie a pebble with Mags standing next to me, I can catch its one strand with hers, park it, and untie that. Her strand's relaxed for a year and a day. Nothing can be shaped onto a relaxed strand. He can't sour her."
Orla wipes her trowel on her knee.
"The docket waits for the untie," she says. "Does the snare, do you suppose?"
I open my mouth to say yes, and then I see the ironmonger's step.

My bob circled five over that step for twelve mornings. The snare had been on it since the Thursday I watched Vosper's hands tie it, weeks before Lenny Pask put his name to anything. The docket comes last. The snare comes first, at the anchor, whenever the seller likes, and a snare binds its recipient the moment it's tied. Relax her afterwards and it still finds her.

"I'm wrong," I say. "A snare binds when it's tied, and it's already tied. He tied the step weeks before anyone signed. He'll have tied hers the same way. An empty keeper's line doesn't mean an empty site."
"No," says Orla. "It doesn't."
"So relaxing her wouldn't shield her. It would only be one more crime with my name on it." I make myself say the rest. "The only lawful hope is to find the site. Or to be there when it fires."
Orla nods once, and goes back to her weeding.
I promised Mags a day. I'm going to have to give it back to her.
I ring the union hall from the tram stop at the bottom of the allotments. The caretaker answers at last, chewing something.
"She's not in, love. Went off this afternoon with her case."
"Did she say where? It's Ila. Ila Brandt. I was in this morning."
"I know who you are." He swallows. "Said she was going to see a retired member. Said a member had the right. That's all I've got."
"Thank you," I say. "Really. What's your name?"
He tells me it's none of my business, quite cheerfully, and rings off.

The tram comes. I sit by the window with my bob in my fist and Abbot's dirt still under my nails, and I practise what I'm going to say to Mags. I'm wrong, Mags. I was wrong about the docket. I don't get past the first sentence, because every time I get there I'm back on the step, with my bob going round and round over a snare I didn't know how to see.
It's nearly dark when I come up the row of lock-ups off Tallow Row. Ours is the last one. The door is rolled half up and the light's on, and there are two voices inside, and one of them is Mags.
I stop by the next door along, where the light doesn't reach.
"Pass us the spoke key," Dad says.
"Aurel."
"It's on your side. By the tin."
"Aurel."
The ratchet stops. For a while there's only the hiss of the paraffin heater and the tick of a wheel turning slowly on its own.
"Triple," my father says. "Once. Triple rate, and told not to ask, and I didn't ask. That's all there was to it."
"Did you know?"
"I didn't know there was anybody in it." His voice is very quiet. "Mags. Nobody said there was anybody in it. I'd never have put my hand to it. Never."
Inside what? I know inside what. I've just spent eleven days waiting to read about it. I stand in the dark and don't let myself finish the thought, and it finishes itself anyway.
I step into the light.

Dad is on his stool with a wheel clamped between his knees, the way he always is, and he doesn't look up. Behind him my chalk map of Brindlemouth covers the whole back wall. Mags is standing by the bench. She doesn't look surprised to see me. I think she knew I'd come.
"A retired member has the right to hear it first," she says. "That's the rule, and I keep it."
"Inspector," says Dad, to the wheel.
Mags's document case is open on the bench. The blue carbon card is lying on top, the bottom third still folded under along the crease she made this morning.
Nobody stops me. Mags could. She lays her palm flat on the bench instead, next to the card, not on it.
I pick it up and unfold the keeper's line.

The signature has come through the carbon upright and steady, every letter pressed evenly from both sides, the way you only write when one hand holds the card flat while the other one signs. I have never seen my father write like that in my life. I didn't know he ever could.
Keeper: Aurel Brandt.
